newsitem.title: TURKEY: TURKEY FORMS ANTI-MONOPOLY BOARD, NAMES CHAIRMAN.
newsitem.headline: TURKEY FORMS ANTI-MONOPOLY BOARD, NAMES CHAIRMAN.

text.p: Turkey formed a long-awaited anti-monopoly board, required as part of its customs union pact with the European Union and named economics professor Aydin Ayaydin as the chairman, the official gazette said on Thursday.
The 11-member board will implement an anti-monopoly law, awaited since the customs deal took effect in January 1996.

"In fact, this was a belated decision. The law was passed 2-1/2 years ago, but was not put into effect as the board could not be formed. This a very positive development for Turkey in the transition period for future full membership in the EU," Ayaydin told Reuters.
He said the board's practices would also have important impacts on the Turkish economy by preventing companies from acting as monopolies in the domestic markets.
The anti-monopoly law bans any attempts, agreements or actions that could directly or indirectly obstruct, spoil or restrict competition in goods and services.

"Once the law is implemented, the European countries will not be able to impose anti-dumping duties on Turkish exports which harmed our trade with Europe, mainly after the customs union," Ayaydin said.
"I expect the exports to rise and their quality to improve," he added.
Ayaydin said the board was likely to hold its first meeting next week to start preparing regulations in line with the law.

The latest official figures showed Turkey's trade deficit with the EU rose 32 percent to $804 million in the first half of 1996 from $608.2 million in the same 1995 period, despite previous expectations of an export boom.
The release of trade data has been delayed due to technical difficulties caused by the customs union.

The customs union agreement was weakened by a lack of political will in Turkey to develop EU relations and reluctance to pass a new tax system in line with the EU after the formation of an Islamist-led coalition in June 1996.
On the other hand, the European Parliament froze financial aid to Turkey last year, including MEDA funds, citing lack of improvement in its human rights record.
